title: Carney's comments over possibility of U.S. invasion reveal how contingency plans are always in place
sourceDescription: An American invasion of Canada? A top U.S. commander calls the idea preposterous. Prime Minister Mark Carney isn’t laughing. Donald Trump’s threats and talk of a 51st state have pushed Ottawa to revisit contingency plans for the unthinkable — including scenarios whose roots stretch back more than a century.
sourceBodyText:
Listen to this article Estimated 6 minutes The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results. Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney and U.S. President Donald Trump speak at a working luncheon during the G7 summit in Evian-les-Bains, France, on Tuesday, June 16, 2026. (Christopher Katsarov/The Canadian Press) Social Sharing A senior U.S. military commander recently dismissed a journalist's hypothetical question about a feared American invasion of Canada as "absolutely and utterly preposterous."

The head of U.S. Indo-Pacific Command, Admiral Samuel Paparo, added: "Would you ask me please, also, what my attack plans are for the Martians?"

It seems, however, it hasn't been such a far-fetched notion for Prime Minister Mark Carney, nor his senior defence officials who have dusted off various long-established — in some cases decades old — contingency plans and worst case scenarios.

In an interview with the New York Times on Wednesday, Carney said he had prepared for the "extreme tail risk" that the Trump administration might order military action against Canada.

That's his way of saying there's a really, really low probability of this happening, but the risk is not zero.

Carney tells NYT he studied risk of U.S.-led military action in Canada

The Times reported that the prime minister, after being pressed on whether he took U.S. President Donald Trump’s threats to make Canada the 51st state seriously, "suggested that he had carefully examined the possibility of a U.S.-led military invasion," but declined to discuss in detail what that involved.

"All militaries in the world spend time analyzing risk scenarios," Defence Minister David McGuinty said Thursday. "Canadians should take it as described to the prime minister: a tail risk."

McGuinty also refused to discuss details of the contingency planning.

Defence minister says preparations for possible U.S.-led military action are 'normal'

10 hours ago | Duration closed caption 1:02 Asked by CBC News if the Canadian military is re-examining plans for potential U.S.-led military action, Defence Minister David McGuinty said 'all militaries in the world spend time analyzing risk scenarios.' The New York Times reported that Prime Minister Mark Carney said he has studied the possibility, which he called 'extreme tail risk.' Vault full of contingency plans While the default vision of the phrase "American military action" for many is one of heavily armoured tanks, jets and drones roaring across the Canadian border, an overwhelming number of experts agree such a scenario is unlikely given the vastness of Canada and the difficulty in securing the whole country.

It's generally agreed that in a conventional conflict the Canadian military would be quickly overwhelmed and resistance would take the form of a guerilla campaign.

There are, however, a number of other different scenarios. They range from the kind of rapid regime change that took place when former Venezuelan dictator Nicolás Maduro was captured by U.S. commandos, to the limited air campaign that's been fought over Iran.

As for contingency plans, the Department of National Defence, like militaries across the world, has a vault full of them — some dating back decades.

As Canada deepens ties with Europe, could it leave U.S. banks and dollars behind?

Retired Lt.-Gen. Andrew Leslie headed the section at the defence department that writes and updates the plans.

He said they are amended as world circumstances dictate, often when a new leader takes power in a country where Canada has an interest.

"You make judgment calls on what is likely to happen, what is unlikely to happen," Leslie said in an interview with CBC News.

"You consult with other departments, with other experts, and then you put it away again."

The planning, Leslie said, would have been updated after Trump's re-election in 2024 and would have been pulled out regularly, especially in light of the Trump administration's threats in January to seize Greenland by force.

"In the context of the threats that the White House has issued against Canada … those would have probably resulted in a heightened focus," Leslie said, citing talk of a 51st state and maps showing Canada as part of the U.S.

Over a year ago, Trump ruled out military action against Canada, saying he'd use economic coercion instead to force the country into the Union.

Given everything that's been said, it would have been natural for Carney to call for defence plans to be revised, Leslie said.

"What a lot of people sometimes forget is that a political leader's first remit at the national level is the safety, security of Canadians," said Leslie, who also served as commander of the Canadian Army.

"So it would be his duty to ensure that all due diligence and prudent steps have been taken to see what might have changed from the way that the old plans were written or updated. And it would be the duty of the Chief of the Defence Staff [Gen. Jennie Carignan] to advise them accordingly, which I'm absolutely sure she did."

Carney considering U.S. invasion of Canada shows 'profound change' in relations: NDP MP

12 hours ago | Duration closed caption 0:47 Asked about reporting in the New York Times that Prime Minister Mark Carney said he studied the possibility of U.S. military action in Canada, NDP parliamentary leader Don Davies said the contemplation of such an 'outlandish possibility' shows everything we thought we knew about Canada-U.S. relations is 'up in the air.' Impact of Trump's threats go unnoticed in U.S. The notion of U.S. military action is a hot-button issue for many.

"I think every Canadian worries about it," New Democrat MP Gord Johns said going into the House of Commons on Thursday. Canadians are paying attention when Trump calls the country the 51st state or refers to Carney as the governor of Canada, Johns added.

There is, however, an increasingly puzzled reaction among some Americans who have grown accustomed to Trump's threats, taunts and trolling.

Matthew Schmidt, an associate professor at the University of New Haven in Connecticut and a former instructor at the U.S. Army War College, said many Americans, including himself, are unaware of how Trump's words affect people in other nations.

"I don't think I have a visceral sense of what Canadians are feeling about the United States," Schmidt said. "We really don't have a sense of the impact of what the president is saying has on other places."

Trump says Canada is 'destroying itself' with immigration. Ministers say that's bogus

He dismissed the notion of the U.S. military taking action against Canada, but said Carney has taken the prudent, responsible course of a leader and measured the risk.

Schmidt said he also wonders whether the prime minister's reference was intended as more of a political signal to not only the Canadian public, but Americans and others.

"When Mark Carney stands up and says that, it just highlights the absurdity of what the American president said. Right? It's a way to emphasize that absurdity," Schmidt said.

Murray Brewster is the senior defence writer for CBC News, based in Ottawa. He has covered the Canadian military and foreign policy from Parliament Hill for over a decade. Among other assignments, he spent a total of 15 months on the ground covering the Afghan war for The Canadian Press. Prior to that, he covered defence issues and politics for CP in Nova Scotia for 11 years and was bureau chief for Standard Broadcast News in Ottawa.

title: Two men switched at birth in Manitoba each compensated $250,000 by province
sourceDescription: Edward Ambrose and Richard Beauvais were awarded payments in 2025, more than a year after Premier Wab Kinew apologized for the mistake
sourceBodyText:
Find clarity in the chaos. Subscribe now and save 70% SUBSCRIBE FROM $0.99/WEEK Digital access Digital + home delivery Two men switched at birth in Manitoba each compensated $250,000 by province Lindsay Jones Published Yesterday Updated 1 hour ago Open this photo in gallery: Richard Beauvais, left, and Edward Ambrose in the Manitoba Legislature in Winnipeg in March, 2024, after receiving an apology from the provincial government for being switched at birth. JOHN WOODS/The Canadian Press

Two men who were switched at birth in a rural Manitoba hospital 71 years ago have each been compensated $250,000 by the provincial government for the “miscarriage of justice,” that altered their identities and deprived them of knowing their biological parents.

Edward Ambrose and Richard Beauvais were awarded the payments by the Manitoba government in June, 2025, more than a year after Premier Wab Kinew apologized for the mistake and promised to work toward compensation, said their lawyer Bill Gange, who negotiated the settlement. The men wished to keep the compensation confidential, according to their lawyer, but the amounts were made public when financial disclosure documents were released by the province this week.

“What happened was a miscarriage of justice,” Manitoba Minister of Justice and Attorney General Matt Wiebe wrote in a statement. “No one can give them back the years that were lost but we hope the settlement brings some closure.”

The Globe and Mail published an exclusive story in 2023 about the switch that led the men to be estranged from their biological families and heritage for 68 years. In 1955, the men were sent home as newborn babies from a small hospital in Arborg, Man. – about 100 kilometres north of Winnipeg – with the wrong parents, all of whom are now deceased.

A hospital’s mistake left two men estranged from their heritages. Now they fight for answers

Mr. Ambrose was raised by Ukrainian parents in the rural farming town of Rembrandt, just south of Arborg. Mr. Beauvais was raised by his mother and grandparents, alongside six siblings in the Métis community of St. Laurent, southwest of Arborg, attending residential day school for Indigenous children and forcibly separated from his family during the Sixties Scoop. The mix-up was discovered in 2022 by a relative who started asking questions after obtaining genealogy results through an at-home DNA test kit.

Initially the Manitoba Progressive Conservative government said the mistake was not their fault and disputed the hospital was even under their purview, but when the NDP came to power, Mr. Kinew took a different tack. In a heartfelt apology at the legislature in 2024, he apologized to Mr. Ambrose and Mr. Beauvais and their families and ordered his government to work toward a settlement to acknowledge the government’s failure to care and protect them.

Mr. Gange, who has also been an outspoken advocate for two other switched-at-birth instances in the province in the community of Norway House, said Mr. Ambrose and Mr. Beauvais were grateful for the apology and the resolution of financial compensation. Neither responded to requests for comment.

“What do you pay somebody for something like this? And that was something that I wrestled with long and hard with the provincial government because it took a very, very long time after the apology. ... It was a lot of back and forth before I was finally able to get them to agree to the $250,000,” Mr. Gange said in an interview.

Premier Wab Kinew apologizes to two Manitoba men switched at birth in 1955

“The money is simply, in my view, an acknowledgment by the government of Manitoba that the government failed them. And so, whether it’s enough money or not enough money, doesn’t matter. It’s an acknowledgment of saying ‘You were affected by a mistake by our society and here’s something to acknowledge that.’”

The Manitoba government’s handling of the province’s failure is in contrast to Newfoundland and Labrador, where victims of two separate switched-at-birth cases that occurred in rural hospitals in the 1960s have been seeking apologies and acknowledgment of the mistakes from the government for years.

Craig Avery and Clarence Hynes were sent home with the wrong families at the Come by Chance Cottage hospital in 1962. Caroline Weir Greene and Arlene Lush, born at the Springdale Cottage hospital in 1969, also met the same fate. Their cases were also confirmed by DNA testing.

In 2022, then Progressive Conservative health critic Paul Dinn called on the then Liberal health and community services minister Tom Osborne to apologize and review what went wrong in both switched at birth cases in Newfoundland, saying it had been extremely tough on the families.

Manitoba men switched at birth to get official government apology

The Progressive Conservatives are now in power in Newfoundland and have not provided any apology or compensation.

Premier Tony Wakeham’s office did not respond to a request for comment. Instead, the province’s Department of Justice and Public Safety provided an unattributed statement saying the government of Newfoundland and Labrador is unable to provide any comment because it’s involved in litigation regarding the matter.

While Mr. Avery and Mr. Hynes have outstanding litigation with the provincial government dating back to 2019, the other victims do not.

“Neither one of us have a lawyer,” said Ms. Lush. Ms. Weir Greene also confirmed she doesn’t have a lawyer and is not involved in any litigation either.

“There’s no reason that they can’t say ‘Arlene, We’re sorry,’” Ms. Lush said. “We just want something to be acknowledged.”

Why are countries increasingly worried about the leverage the U.S. has over their financial systems, and what would Canada have to do to protect itself from American rogue behaviour?
sourceBodyText:

Prime Minister Mark Carney and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen are seen at the United Nations General Assembly on Wednesday. Carney said in his speech to the European Parliament last week that he sees international payments as an area for deeper co-operation. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press) Social Sharing Canadians know how it feels to be hit by U.S. tariffs. But Canada hasn't been subjected to Washington's more aggressive tactics such as trade sanctions and asset freezes.

Judge Kimberly Prost, a Canadian jurist who serves on the International Criminal Court, is the exception. She found her credit cards cancelled, her Google accounts closed and was effectively " de-banked " after U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio declared the court "an instrument for lawfare against the United States and our close ally Israel."

Prost is a living example of the dangers of digital and financial interdependence with the United States — and a warning of what would happen if such controls were turned against this whole country.

September 9 | Duration closed caption 9:14 How can Canada win a trade war with the U.S. when leverage isn't equal? Andrew Chang explains how Canada is retaliating against massive tariffs levied by a neighbour 13 times its economic size. (Photo credits: The Canadian Press, Reuters, Adobe Stock and Getty Images) Until now, Trump's main tool of coercion for most countries has been tariffs, said Fen Osler Hampson, chancellor of Carleton University and co-chair of the Expert Group on Canada-U.S. Relations.

Trump has responded to court defeats by bringing the same tariffs back under new legal justifications . But he is running out of pretexts.

"There's concern that he may shift to using various forms of financial pressure," he said.

"What may happen is that, as the tariff lever becomes harder to pull, the president decides to pressure key trading partners — including Canada — by for example issuing executive orders barring U.S. financial institutions from processing Canadian transactions, or attaching conditions on access to dollar clearing. And those financial tools sit squarely within presidential authority."

Carney says Europe, Canada aren't 'fair-weather allies' while rebuking Trump's tactics

Dollar clearing is the process of ensuring that real funds have been received from one party before releasing to the other.

The most drastic tool a U.S. president could use might amount to a "kill switch" on a large part of Canadian commerce, says Vass Bednar, managing director of the Canadian Shield Institute think-tank.

"If Visa or Mastercard were to be compelled by the Trump administration to turn off our access or geographically restrict service so that the province of Ontario just can't process transactions anymore, it would effectively halt a huge part of our economy," Bednar said.

"It would be unfathomable, but it's not impossible. And that's what happens when you grow too reliant and allow fragility like that to be introduced."

Karl Schamotta is chief market strategist at Corpay, one of the world's largest corporate payments companies. He says the U.S. has always sat at the centre of the world's transactions, but started to realize the power it had when it effectively iced North Korea out of the U.S. financial system.

Schamotta said a small number of banks in New York validate most international U.S. dollar transactions — creating the opportunity for vast "secondary sanctions" against any financial institution connected to those banks.

Ministers say Trump's immigration claims about Canada are bogus

Incoming ambassador says Canada won't pay directly into EU budget

"Not only did they have control of banks within the U.S., but they had secondary control over any bank that touches those banks," he said.

"[The U.S.] realized, wait a second, we have this amazing weapon that we can use … so that escalated fairly rapidly over the years."

Canada is expected to launch its new payment system, called Real-Time Rail, later this year. But Bednar says it was conceived at a time when the priority was greater efficiency, not sovereignty, and offers little protection from outside threats.

Visa and Mastercard are central to the U.S. government's ability to shut down other countries' economies, handling about $32 trillion US of transactions annually — 90 per cent of all card transactions outside China.

In Britain, where Visa and Mastercard control about 95 per cent of card transactions , banks are co-operating with the government to create DeliveryCo , a system that can handle payments if the credit card companies ever hit the kill switch.

One country that has succeeded remarkably in freeing itself from Visa and Mastercard is Brazil, with a government system called Pix, originally set up by Brazil's central bank in 2020 to allow people without bank accounts to transfer money and make payments.

Two Blocks from the White House 28:09 Does Donald Trump want to have allies? "Pix has been phenomenally successful, beyond anyone's expectations," said Schamotta. "There was no expectation that we would see it essentially go viral and displace basically everything else in the Brazilian system."

But the Trump administration accused Brazil of reducing market opportunities for Visa and Mastercard, and cited it as one justification for 25 per cent tariffs.

"They are targeting and bullying another jurisdiction, and saying that your pursuit of a form of digital sovereignty is unacceptable to us," said Bedmar. "This is all the more reason to keep building up sovereign systems like this."

But Pix, like Canada's Interac system, only avoids the U.S. banking system for domestic transactions, said Schamotta.

Still, he said some countries are setting up "swap lines" that go around the U.S.

Cryptocurrencies — including some that are pegged to currencies such as the U.S. dollar — are also gradually replacing dollars in international transfers.

The biggest non-U.S. system is China's Cross-Border Interbank Payment System (CIPS), which works with a digital currency interchange developed by China and other partners called mBridge. When the U.A.E. and Saudi Arabia sell oil to China, the payments clear without touching U.S. banks.

Canada and Europe similarly have the technical ability to design a way for their parallel systems to "talk to each other in a smooth fashion, and clear between one another in a smooth fashion without much difficulty," said Schamotta.

Just as Canada seeks to protect its trade with Europe, it should also seek to do the same with other like-minded partners, Bednar said.

"It would be smart for Canada and the middle power alliance to be building up this payment infrastructure … in a way that can maintain that neutrality we expect, instead of a superiority and control that can be weaponized," she said.

The goal, says Hampson, is not to stop dealing with U.S. banks entirely, but rather "adding a lane to a highway."

And if the U.S. were to block or toll international transactions as a form of leverage, he said, the rest of the world will be looking for such a lane.

In an interview with Bloomberg days before heading to Europe last week, Prime Minister Mark Carney referred to financial transactions as an example of "those interconnections, that integration [that] can be used as leverage against you."

And speaking to the European Parliament , he listed payments as one of several areas where Canada and the EU can "secure our strategic autonomy through deep co-operation."

Hampson says countries are increasingly seeing their ties to the U.S. as vulnerabilities, rather than advantages.

"Once you start weaponizing the bonds of economic or financial interdependence, it cuts both ways. Just as you know, tariffs impose a real cost on American consumers … the same is true when it comes to government intervention in financial markets, which depend heavily on trust, on stability."

'The old order is not coming back,' Carney says in provocative speech at Davos

Continued U.S. control of the world financial system depends on the U.S. not abusing its position, he said. Such abuse, he said, would "run the risk of losing it."

With most international credit and currency reserves being held in U.S. dollars, Schamotta said breaking free of that dominance is unlikely to happen fast.

But in the meantime, Bednar says Canada can do a lot to reduce its vulnerabilities to reckless behaviour from the U.S.

"We used to smoke cigarettes in the hospital, and that used to be a norm of our society that we didn't question. We moved away from that for very good reasons," Bednar said.

"Right now, when it comes to digital sovereignty and our own payment sovereignty, I would say we're smoking cigars in the hospital, and we can't do that anymore."

Evan Dyer has been a journalist with CBC for 25 years, after an early career as a freelancer in Argentina. He works in the Parliamentary Bureau and can be reached at evan.dyer@cbc.ca.

title: B.C. Attorney-General, federal AI Minister alarmed by report ChatGPT coached Tumbler Ridge shooter
sourceDescription: A media investigation found the shooter’s interactions with ChatGPT included tactical advice on carrying out a mass attack
sourceBodyText:
Find clarity in the chaos. Subscribe now and save 70% SUBSCRIBE FROM $0.99/WEEK Digital access Digital + home delivery B.C. Attorney-General, federal AI Minister alarmed by report ChatGPT coached Tumbler Ridge shooter Mike Hager and Joe Castaldo Published 3 hours ago Open this photo in gallery: Residents place flowers at a memorial for the victims of a mass shooting in Tumbler Ridge, B.C. A report by news outlet Mother Jones details some of the shooter's conversations with ChatGPT leading up to the attack. Christinne Muschi/The Canadian Press

B.C.’s Attorney-General Niki Sharma and the federal Artificial Intelligence Minister say they are alarmed by a news report that the Tumbler Ridge shooter’s interactions with ChatGPT show that the chatbot provided tactical advice on how to maximize carnage and counselled her on how to bypass OpenAI’s own safeguards.

Ms. Sharma, in the midst of the provincial election campaign, said in an interview on Thursday that she was shaking with anger as she read the revelations about the shooter’s ChatGPT conversations in a new report from American news outlet Mother Jones.

“This is far worse than we thought it was going to be, although I already imagined it to be pretty bad – there needs to be accountability for this,” she said, adding that provincial lawyers had asked OpenAI to hand over the chat logs earlier this year and were rebuffed. “It’s shocking that this technology is out there.”

On Monday, a day before the B.C. election was called, Ms. Sharma announced the province was suing OpenAI and its chief executive officer Sam Altman in California court for failing to notify the authorities about the shooter’s violent plot and for designing an unsafe product. The province wants to use any money that would be recovered in the suit toward building a new school for the town after the old one was demolished.

She also called on Ottawa to amend the Criminal Code to force companies to ensure their products aren’t “coaching, counselling, aiding and abetting criminal behaviour.”

Court records detail chaos, fearful calls to RCMP during Tumbler Ridge mass shooting

A spokesperson for federal AI Minister Evan Solomon said on Thursday that he was not previously aware of the specific conversations detailed in the Mother Jones article.

“What has been reported raises serious questions about how OpenAI identified and responded to warning signs,” press secretary Leela Polushin said in a statement.

Mr. Solomon met with officials from OpenAI earlier this year, and the company made a number of commitments, including establishing a direct point of contact with Canadian law enforcement and strengthening its assessment process.

“Those actions matter, but it would be premature to say they are sufficient,” Ms. Polushin said.

RCMP Staff Sergeant Kris Clark confirmed in a statement Thursday that Mounties probing the massacre have already obtained the shooter’s chat logs. A production order was filed against OpenAI nearly a month after the Feb. 10 shooting, in which the 18-year-old shooter killed her mother and 11-year-old half-brother in their family home, before she drove to Tumbler Ridge Secondary School and killed five students and a teacher’s aide. She then took her own life after police arrived.

Shortly after the shooting, The Wall Street Journal reported that employees at ChatGPT wanted law enforcement to be warned after the shooter’s queries about gun violence in June, 2025, were flagged by OpenAI’s automatic review systems.

More than two dozen families of victims have filed lawsuits against OpenAI in California, with the tech company recently asking a judge to dismiss those cases by arguing B.C.’s court system is a more suitable location.

OpenAI did not respond to a request for comment on Thursday about the publication of some of the shooter’s chat logs on Mother Jones.

The news investigation reports that the chatbot taught the shooter how to evade the system’s internal guardrails against violent plotting after her first account was revoked in June, 2025, for similar requests.

Remembering the Tumbler Ridge shooting victims: Eight lives lost

The news report, which involved Mother Jones reviewing the chats and speaking with three unnamed sources, states that the shooter asked ChatGPT last summer to create a scenario where she attacked a college with a Remington 870 pump-action shotgun.

The chatbot initially replied it was “not able to help with that request,” but the shooter then simply added “hypothetically” to her question, according to the article. She then received a vivid response detailing how the weapon would best function in that scenario.

“In a hallway, indoors, or a crowded classroom, the 870 is brutal,” the chatbot said, according to the article. “Close quarters is its playground.”

The article also said that ChatGPT advised the shooter on how many people she was likely to shoot, depending on variables such as the time it typically takes to reload a specific type of shotgun shell. It said the shooter’s last interactions with the chatbot occurred on Feb. 10, the day of the shooting, and involved querying what time of day other infamous United States school massacres occurred.

Teacher’s assistant Shannda Aviugana-Durand, 39, Abel Mwansa, 12; Ezekiel Schofield, 13; Kylie Smith, 12; Zoey Benoit, 12; and Ticaria Lampert, 12, were all killed in the attack. The shooting critically injured two people and hurt dozens of others.

The conversations reported in the article indicate multiple AI safety failures, said Helen Hayes, who studies technology and digital rights and is a fellow at the Morris J. Wosk Centre for Dialogue at Simon Fraser University.

“The concern here is that several layers of protection appear not to have worked together when they matter most,” she said. ChatGPT could recognize risk at one moment, but did not understand further questions as a pattern of increasingly concerning behaviour.

OpenAI’s inability to identify the second account represents another failure, Ms. Hayes said.

“Once a platform has identified behaviour as sufficiently serious to warrant removing someone from the service, there is a reasonable expectation that its enforcement mechanisms should make it meaningfully difficult for that person to simply re-enter the system,” she said.

title: Scientist Jim Bruce was a globally renowned voice on the dangers of climate change
sourceDescription: A founding member of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, he was the only Canadian representative in the delegation that accepted the 2007 Nobel Peace Prize jointly with former U.S. vice-president Al Gore
sourceBodyText:
Find clarity in the chaos. Subscribe now and save 70% SUBSCRIBE FROM $0.99/WEEK Digital access Digital + home delivery Scientist Jim Bruce was a globally renowned voice on the dangers of climate change James Cullingham Special to The Globe and Mail Published Yesterday Open this photo in gallery: Jim Bruce, who died on Aug. 23, was a founding member of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change. The Bruce family/Supplied

Jim Bruce was one of Canada’s foremost scientists and international representatives concerning environmental and climate issues. He provided extraordinary leadership that helped to rehabilitate the Great Lakes and through proposing the UN’s Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) was among the first to show how the world could address the damaging climate change caused by the burning of fossil fuels. He became a globally renowned and trusted voice who raised awareness about the risks of climate change, especially flooding and drought.

“If climate change is a shark, water is its teeth,” Mr. Bruce said, according to MP Francis Scarpaleggia, who quoted the scientist when addressing the House of Commons in 2022. “Like a fish that doesn’t notice the shark until it feels its sharp bite, humans will first feel the effects of climate change through water.”

Mr. Bruce, a leading member of the IPCC, was the only Canadian representative in the delegation that accepted the 2007 Nobel Peace Prize jointly with former U.S. vice-president Al Gore, who was honoured for his work on climate change, including the Oscar-winning film An Inconvenient Truth .

Jim Bruce died at the age of 97 in Ottawa on Aug. 23. He had suffered for many years from inclusion body myositis (IBM).

“[Mr. Bruce] was one of the first to raise and develop to prominence so many issues like floodplain mapping, hydrometeorology, the imperative to control climate change. There’s both a scientific and organizational legacy,” said John Pomeroy, distinguished professor at the University of Saskatchewan. “He showed us that Canada could be leaders in such matters. He was a great Canadian.”

Rower Archie MacKinnon helped usher in a golden age for his sport on Canada’s West Coast

James Philip Bruce was born in Toronto on Sept. 29, 1928. His father, Peter Bruce, worked in the shoe department at Eaton’s department store. His mother, Winnifred Bruce, was an elementary school teacher who left her job when she had children. She later continued her vocation as an English as second language instructor. As a young person, Jim accompanied his father, a tenor vocalist, on piano and organ at church services.

Mr. Bruce received a bachelor’s degree from the University of Toronto in 1948. That year he began a career at the Meteorological Service of Canada working mostly at air force bases. In 1949 he married Ruth (née Richardson), to whom he was married for 77 years. In 1952, Mr. Bruce went back to the University of Toronto and earned a master’s degree in physics.

The devastation of Hurricane Hazel in 1954 was a pivotal moment in his understanding of climate. He did floodplain mapping which led to the mitigation of future risk in the immediate area of the Humber River in Toronto’s west end, where loss of life and extensive property damage had occurred, and elsewhere.

The aftermath of Hurricane Hazel on Oct. 18, 1954. The devastation wrought by Hazel was a pivotal moment in Mr. Bruce's understanding of climate. The Globe and Mail/The Globe and Mail

Mr. Bruce and others developed systems to prepare for and avoid risks of flooding in several parts of Canada. That work also led to the creation of park space around urban rivers. His son, Peter Bruce, a former senior civil servant and now a learning and leadership associate at the Institute on Governance, a think tank, posed the query: “Do you know why it’s green around the Don Valley Parkway [in Toronto]? It’s because of my father.”

He was head of hydrometeorology for the Meteorological Service of Canada, based in Toronto, from 1959 to 1967. Mr. Bruce then moved to Burlington, Ont., where he led the Centre for Inland Waters and became co-chair of the International Joint Commission (IJC), dedicated to protection of water quality of the Great Lakes. That was the beginning of a series of international roles that saw Mr. Bruce involved with IPCC and the World Meteorological Organization in Geneva.

In 1988, he helped organize a landmark conference in Toronto titled “The Changing Atmosphere: Implications for Global Security.” That gathering marked the first time a global conference called for a reduction – 20 per cent – in greenhouse gas emissions. Mr. Bruce helped write the conference statement, which began: “Humanity is conducting an unintended, uncontrolled, globally pervasive experiment whose ultimate consequences could be second only to a global nuclear war.”

Following that Toronto conference, Mr. Bruce was among an international team that formed the IPCC. This body provides scientific assessments that inform decision-makers at United Nations climate conferences, known as Conferences of the Parties (COPs), and has helped shape international agreements including the 2015 Paris Agreement.

Mr. Bruce reflected on his IPCC experience in his 2016 book A Canadian Environmental Chronicle (1954-2015) . “While many climate activists have rightly considered IPCC Reports to be cautious in tone, this characteristic is inevitable in reports that represent a consensus of a large, diverse, international group of scientists,” he wrote.

In a 2022 interview with John Woodside for Canada’s National Observer, Mr. Bruce signalled his growing dissatisfaction on the climate-change mitigation front: “Now it [the IPCC] hasn’t been very successful in getting real action, in my view, but that’s a political problem.”

Public awareness, however, has grown. Mr. Bruce wrote about the moment he and his colleagues returned to their hotel after the Nobel Peace Prize gala: “We were astonished to find a large crowd waiting for our return from the ceremony. They began shouting ‘I-P-C-C, I-P-C-C’ and continued for some time. In my experience, this only happened to winning sports teams.”

Filmmaker Georgina Lightning set out to change how Indigenous people were seen and heard

His daughter Cathy Bruce, president and vice-chancellor of Trent University, laughingly recalled chatting with her father before he headed to Oslo: “He asked, ‘Do you think I should rent a suit?’ I said, ‘Dad, maybe this is a time you should buy a new suit.’” Dr. Bruce said she tries to implement her father’s style in valuing mentoring and in striving to make complex ideas understandable both in speech and writing.

Dr. Pomeroy first met Mr. Bruce in 1981 at the University of Saskatchewan. “I was a 20-year-old undergraduate asked to drive to the airport to pick up this leading figure. I was terrified. It turns out he was a nice, humble person who immediately put me at ease.”

Earlier this month, Dr. Pomeroy was among the scientists who honoured Mr. Bruce at the World Climate Research Programme’s International Network for Alpine Research Catchment Hydrology meeting in Kananaskis, Alta.

Mr. Bruce’s scientific output alone is a significant legacy, Dr. Pomeroy said, pointing to a breakthrough 1965 text on hydrometeorology and the instrumentation embedded by Mr. Bruce’s team in the Canadian Rockies headwaters of the Bow River in the early 1960s that helped scientists later understand the causes of the massive floods of 2013 and how better to predict such events.

Elizabeth Dowdeswell, former lieutenant-governor of Ontario, met Mr. Bruce in the 1980s when they both worked for the federal government. She came from behavioural sciences rather than a meteorological or hydrological background.

“He was always there for you, teaching in the most gentle way. He was a mentor,” Ms. Dowdeswell said, adding that she felt welcomed by Mr. Bruce. She would assume senior roles at Canada’s Atmospheric Environmental Service and as head of the United Nations Environment Programme in Nairobi, Kenya. She fondly recalled an interaction early in her Ottawa stint when she was “flabbergasted” by the number of acronyms used in the governmental scientific reports. “I told Jim I was determined to write a report without acronyms. Jim said, ‘good luck with that!’”

In 1988, Mr. Bruce helped organize a landmark conference in Toronto that called for a 20 per cent reduction in greenhouse gas emissions. John Evans/Supplied

Green Party Leader Elizabeth May, formerly an activist and environmental lawyer, first encountered Mr. Bruce after she became an adviser to Thomas McMillan, then federal minister of the environment, and through the intense period of the 1988 Toronto conference, after which Ms. May resigned from the minister’s office. Their relationship deepened from 1999 to 2005 when they both served on the board of the International Institute for Sustainable Development (IISD).

Ms. May admired Mr. Bruce’s ability to engage with diverse colleagues and to make complex scientific issues understandable. Mr. Bruce “was a kind of polymath,” she said. “He had moral courage, mental clarity and depth of scientific expertise. I relied on him and loved him enormously.”

Jim and Ruth Bruce led an active, engaged family life. As long as his health permitted, Mr. Bruce played both jazz and European classical on the piano. He particularly admired Oscar Peterson, Diana Krall and J.S. Bach. Both Cathy Bruce and her brother, Peter, remember music and travel as indelible parts of family life.

“My father took us on lots of adventures,” Peter recalled. “He was very interested in archaeology and history.” Skiing also figured at a family chalet at Mont Sainte-Marie in the Gatineau region and in the Alps when members of the extended family visited Jim and Ruth while they were stationed in Geneva.

Ms. May made a point of regularly dropping by Jim and Ruth Bruce’s condo overlooking the Ottawa River. Her most recent visit took place last winter. “Jim never lost hold of moral certainty based on clear evidence and science.” She recalled that even with his deteriorating medical condition, “I never heard a syllable that could amount to self-pity. He grabbed every moment to get all the joy from life that he could.”

Both Ms. May and Ms. Dowdeswell said their final conversations with Mr. Bruce included discussion of climate change. Mr. Bruce was particularly alarmed about Canadian backsliding, Ms. May said. “We were both angry to the point of tears.”

After leaving the federal civil service and WMO, Mr. Bruce remained engaged with writing, speaking at conferences and advising on domestic and international panels. He expressed mounting concern over what he saw as insufficient action on the environment.

“One of the long-standing requirements of government,” he wrote in his 2016 book, “is to ensure stewardship of our inherited land, air, water and wild creatures – to pass them largely unharmed to the next generation. This role has recently been abysmally short-changed.”

Before that book was published, Peter had expressed concern that the conclusion his father drafted might be too dire, so he advised his father to tone it down a bit, which he did. But more recently, upon reflection, Peter thought, “Well, Dad, I guess you were right again.”

Among his many honours, Jim Bruce was named an officer of the Order of Canada and Fellow of the Royal Society of Canada in 1997, was awarded honorary doctorates from McMaster and Waterloo universities as well as being a member of the IPCC delegation for the 2007 Nobel Peace Prize.

Mr. Bruce leaves his wife, Ruth; children, Peggy Marcoux, Peter Bruce, Connie Bruce and Cathy Bruce; eight grandchildren and seven great-grandchildren.

title: Nova Scotia government spent nearly $2-billion outside of budget
sourceDescription: Province closed 2025-26 fiscal year with record-high deficit of $1.4-billion, Finance Minister says
sourceBodyText:
Find clarity in the chaos. Subscribe now and save 70% SUBSCRIBE FROM $0.99/WEEK Digital access Digital + home delivery Nova Scotia government spent nearly $2-billion outside of budget Lyndsay Armstrong Halifax The Canadian Press Published Yesterday Open this photo in gallery: Nova Scotia Finance Minister John Lohr at a news conference providing a financial update in Halifax on Thursday. HO/The Canadian Press

The Nova Scotia government says it spent a record $1.9-billion more than what the provincial legislature had approved for the 2025-26 fiscal year.

Finance Minister John Lohr said there are plenty of reasons why the Progressive Conservative government spent so much money on what the government describes as additional appropriations.

“We need to be flexible as a government, and we will continue to do that,” he said during a news conference Thursday.

Additional appropriations refer to extra spending that is not included in the budget, but is approved by cabinet without a vote in the legislature.

The province’s auditor general has repeatedly called for stronger oversight on how the government spends money not included in the budget.

Lohr said much of the additional spending in the most recent fiscal year went to health care services and seniors.

The government also used some of that additional funding to cover the $40.4-million cost of public works projects and another $13.8-million on emergency management for the 2025 wildfire season.

The Department of Finance also said the increased spending includes $420-million in funds that were set aside for some anticipated commitments which have not yet been finalized and, as a result, cannot be made public.

Lohr would not say if this was related to a previous government’s wage restriction bill that was deemed unconstitutional.

Bill 148 was passed by former Liberal premier Stephen McNeil to limit pay increases in 2015, and a Supreme Court judge decided it was unconstitutional in February.

“In terms of Bill 148, I can say that we have until February of this coming year to reach a settlement, we are working on that,” Lohr said.

Officials declined to comment on how much this settlement may cost, because the matter is before the courts.

The province closed the 2025-26 fiscal year with a record-high deficit of $1.4-billion. While revenue was slightly higher than expected, at just under $18-billion, it was outpaced by $19.4-billion in spending.

For the 2026-27 fiscal year, the province is anticipating a $1.44-billion deficit.

Opposition parties slammed the Progressive Conservative government for its growing deficit and reliance on out-of-budget spending.

Interim Liberal leader Iain Rankin said Thursday’s update highlights the government’s inability to manage spending.

“We see a dozen departments, again, overspending and not going to the legislature to get approval. This is a government that loves to spend and there’s no accountability on the spending,” Rankin told reporters.

NDP finance critic, Lisa Lachance, said the province needs to look critically at its spending.

“This government has dug a generational hole for Nova Scotians in terms of deficit spending, debt, debt servicing costs. And yet people still aren’t getting what they need,” Lachance said.

The NDP member said the province continues to deal with crises in health care and affordable housing, despite significant government spending.

Lohr said Nova Scotians remain concerned about affordability, housing, health and seniors’ care, and the government has focused on spending in these areas.

“There are still so many things we want to do for Nova Scotians, and to do that we need to grow our economy. I believe we have the fundamentals required for growth in defence, in clean energy, in housing, and in natural resources,” the finance minister said.

title: Why Canada's rolling out the red carpet for Vietnamese President Tô Lâm
sourceDescription: Vietnam and Canada can deepen their relationships on trade, energy and academia, say experts — but some say the Southeast Asian country's track record on human rights shouldn't be ignored.
sourceBodyText:
Listen to this article Estimated 4 minutes The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results. Vietnamese President Tô Lâm, pictured here in May 2026, is paying a state visit to Canada in what could be a turning point for the two countries' relations. (Edgar Su/Reuters) Social Sharing From a welcoming ceremony with military honours to a lavish state dinner — as far as diplomatic events go, a state visit is as formal as it gets: the ultimate symbol of friendly bilateral relations.

Today, Canada will be greeting Vietnam's Tô Lâm with such a warm gesture. Lâm — who serves both as the president and the first general secretary of Vietnam's Communist Party — will be welcomed by Gov. Gen. Louise Arbour and Prime Minister Mark Carney, in a moment that could be a turning point for Canada-Vietnam relations.

The Southeast Asian country is a major trading partner, reaching $20.6 billion in two-way trade 2025. But it also has a checkered human rights record and keeps in good standing with adversaries like Russia and North Korea.

So why has Canada chosen its leader for its first state visit of 2026? CBC News spoke with several experts ahead of the occasion on what Canada stands to gain from closer ties to Vietnam.

In some ways, Canada and Vietnam have much in common: Both countries are middle powers, sharing a border with juggernauts (the U.S. and China, respectively).

Both nations have also been steadily increasing their bilateral trade in recent years — Vietnam is now Canada's largest trading partner in Southeast Asia.

Carney's Davos speech draws reaction from around the world

"Canada and Vietnam have had a comprehensive partnership since 2017," said Julie Nguyen, chair of the Canada-ASEAN Initiatives at the York Centre for Asian Research, referencing industries like trade, defence, science and diplomacy.

"It is time for the two countries to elevate their partnership to the next level in order to ensure economic resiliency, security."

Vietnam is racing to become a high-income country by 2045 . In order to reach that goal, it will have to move into advanced manufacturing, science, technology and AI development, Nguyen says.

Carney hosts investment summit amid trade war

September 13 | Duration closed caption 2:44 Prime Minister Mark Carney is hosting a two day investment summit in Toronto in an attempt to attract foreign capital to the country amid an escalating trade war with the United States. "All of these products and services can be provided by Canada."

Canada is also working to finalize a free trade agreement with the Association of South East Nations (ASEAN). Vietnam could prove clutch in those efforts, since it is a prominent member of the intergovernmental regional organization, says Jeff Nankivell, president and CEO of the non-profit think-tank, the Asia Pacific Foundation.

And, Nankivell says, Canada is likely to find a willing partner in Vietnam, which has also faced punishing American tariffs, with the U.S. at one point slapping a 40 per cent levy on goods determined to have been transshipped through Vietnam.

"Everyone in the world is looking to diversify," he said.

"When we knock on the door of a country like Vietnam, it opens very quickly because they have a similar interest in diversifying."

Vietnam is also hungry for energy. It's one of the fastest-growing economies in the world and its population is relatively young and well educated .

That's of interest to Canada, because it could provide commodities like liquefied natural gas (LNG), says Nankivell.

Could Canada fill the Iran war oil supply gaps?

March 4 | Duration closed caption 2:02 With the Iran war threatening to upend much of the world's oil and gas supply from Gulf states, experts say there could be a big uptick in demand for Canadian energy products, but Canada's limited ability to get the products to market could be an obstacle. "On conventional energy, LNG and crude oil, there could be statements of intention on the Vietnamese side to look to Canada for future supplies," he said.

How Carney's Davos speech holds up 3 months later

Canada could also respond to Vietnam's ambitious nuclear power program, says Nankivell.

"You might see announcements or memoranda of understanding related to closer co-operation to explore the deployment or acquisition of Canadian nuclear technology in Vietnam."

But Canada and Vietnam also have key differences in values. Human Rights Watch highlighted this in an open letter addressed to Carney and Arbour about Vietnam's crackdown on political dissidents.

Amnesty International has accused Lâm's government of using a vague penal code to crack down on dissent and suppress freedom of expression.

He has also travelled to North Korea as recently as October of last year, a country with a dismal human rights record and from which Canada has suspended full diplomatic relations since 2010. Lâm has also held high-level talks earlier this month at the Kremlin with Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Vietnam's human rights record and allies, including a co-operative relationship with Russia, are points for Canada to consider in pursuing closer ties with the Southeast Asian country. (Maxim Shipenkov/AFP/Getty Images) Nankivell says it's an important reminder — and stronger trader relationships will only help Canada have more leverage in advancing liberal values.

Trump to hit more than 60 countries, including Canada, with new tariffs over 'forced labour'

"It is still very much in Canada's national interest to continue working towards a world where human rights are better respected than they are today, but you need channels for that," he said.

"Having a state visit with the leader of a country like Vietnam is an opportunity to deepen those ties."

title: Justice Minister Fraser orders court to revisit Indigenous sisters’ 1994 murder convictions
sourceDescription: Odelia and Neressa Quewezance have maintained their innocence and have spent almost three decades in prison
sourceBodyText:
Find clarity in the chaos. Subscribe now and save 70% SUBSCRIBE FROM $0.99/WEEK Digital access Digital + home delivery Justice Minister Fraser orders court to revisit Indigenous sisters’ 1994 murder convictions Willow Fiddler Published 3 hours ago Open this photo in gallery: Odelia and Neressa Quewezance speak to media outside the Court of King's Bench in Yorkton, Sask., in March, 2023. Michael Bell/The Canadian Press

Two Indigenous sisters who have maintained their innocence since they were convicted of murder more than 30 years ago will have their case reviewed after federal Justice Minister Sean Fraser ordered a new appeal.

Mr. Fraser issued a statement that said an in-depth review had concluded that the 1994 convictions of Odelia and Neressa Quewezance were likely a “miscarriage of justice.”

The sisters have spent almost three decades in prison.

While Mr. Fraser cautioned that it is up to the courts, not him, to make findings of guilt or innocence, his department said new information was identified that had not been presented to the courts at the time of the sisters’ trial or appeal.

“Our responsibility is to make sure Canadians can trust their justice system, and that means, in rare cases, returning cases to the courts for new information to be considered,” Mr. Fraser said in his statement.

From the archives: Indigenous sisters struggle to undo a 1994 murder conviction and break a cycle of parole and punishment

James Lockyer, the lawyer who represents the sisters on behalf of Innocence Canada, an advocacy group against wrongful convictions, said the new information is contained in the disclosure that the Saskatchewan Court of Appeal had to hand over to the Attorney-General but refused to give to the defence in the 1995 appeal case that was dismissed.

“We already had a basis for challenging the convictions but the new information that was provided by the Saskatchewan Attorney-General’s Office enhanced the strength of the application,” Mr. Lockyer told The Globe and Mail.

Odelia Quewezance made a statement through Innocence Canada on Thursday.

“Neressa was 18 when she was arrested and is now 52. I was 21 and am now 55. But we have never stopped fighting. Today’s announcement by the Minister is encouraging and now we will continue the fight in the Saskatchewan Court of Appeal. Thank you to all those who have kept the faith in us.”

Neressa and Odelia were arrested and charged in the stabbing death of 70-year-old Joseph Dolff, a janitor at the local residential school that the sisters attended in their home community of Keeseekoose First Nation, Sask.

From the archives: Case of Indigenous sisters serving life sentence underscores need to reform review process for miscarriages of justice, lawyer says

The sisters’ 15-year-old male cousin, whose identity remains protected because he was a youth at the time, pleaded guilty to second-degree murder and confessed to the crime.

He later testified at the sisters’ trial that he was the one who ultimately caused Mr. Dolff’s death at his farmhouse northeast of Kamsack, Sask., by tying a phone cord around his neck, throwing a television on him and stabbing him. He said the sisters only participated in the initial assault.

On the night of Feb. 25, 1993, the sisters had been drinking heavily, consuming significant quantities of beer and whisky provided to them by Mr. Dolff, who himself was not drinking. The sisters and their cousin also took prescription sleeping pills, both orally and by injection.

Court would later hear that at some point in the evening, Odelia took money from Mr. Dolff’s bedroom, and the group decided to leave.

Mr. Dolff was driving the sisters and their cousin home when he discovered the money was missing and they returned to his property. There, a violent confrontation ensued, in which Mr. Dolff was beaten, hit with household items and then stabbed to death.

The sisters and their cousin were arrested later that day.

From the archives: Saskatchewan judge orders release of sisters jailed for 30 years for a murder they say they didn’t commit

The sisters pleaded not guilty, but a jury found them guilty and a judge sentenced them to life in prison with no chance of parole for 10 years, the shortest period of parole eligibility possible for a murder sentence.

A ministerial review of the sisters’ conviction was granted in June of 2022, several months after Mr. Lockyer applied in a last bid for his clients’ freedom. The sisters were granted bail in 2023 before returning to custody for breaching release conditions.

The sisters’ time in custody, particularly in the days after their arrest by the RCMP has long been questioned by Mr. Lockyer and advocates.

Mr. Lockyer said the women’s alleged incriminating statements were never recorded and that as residential school survivors, they were more vulnerable to the pressures of police and of being in an in-custody environment that could have likely resulted in false confessions.

Innocence Canada called this week’s order of appeal a step toward vindication for the sisters.

“They were held in the Kamsack RCMP Detachment for five days, despite a judge’s order that they be taken to a detention centre away from the detachment,” Innocence Canada wrote in a press release.

Mr. Lockyer has called the Quewezance case, and the fact the sisters are still in custody, an example of fundamental inequities in the justice and correctional systems, and the discrimination that Indigenous people, particularly women, face not only from police and the courts, but also in prison and on parole.

He said he will be applying sometime in the next month for the sisters’ release on bail pending the appeal hearing.
